source_text: DE patientia locuturus, fratres dilectissimi, et utilitates ejus et commoda praedicaturus, unde potius incipiam quam quod nunc quoque ad audientiam vestram patientiam video esse necessariam, ut nec hoc ipsum quod auditis et discitis, sine patientia facere possitis. Tunc enim demum sermo et ratio salutaris efficaciter discitur, si patienter quod dicitur audiatur. Nec invenio, fratres dilectissimi, inter caeteras coelestis disciplinae vias quibus ad consequenda divinitus praemia spei ac fidei nostrae secta dirigitur, quid magis sit vel utilius ad vitam vel majus ad gloriam, quam ut qui praeceptis dominicis obsequio timoris ac devotionis innitimur, patientiam maxime tota observatione tueamur. Hanc se sectari philosophi quoque profitentur. Sed tam illic patientia falsa est, quam et falsa sapientia est. Unde enim vel sapiens esse vel patiens possit qui nec sapientiam nec patientiam Dei novit? quando ipse de his qui sibi sapere in mundo videntur moneat et dicat: Perdam sapientiam sapientium, et prudentiam prudentium reprobabo. Item beatus apostolus Paulus, plenus Spiritu sancto et vocandis formandisque Gentibus missus, contestetur et instruat dicens: Videte ne quis vos depraedetur per philosophiam et inanem fallaciam, secundum traditionem hominum, secundum elementa mundi, et non secundum Christum, quia in ipso habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis. Et alio loco: Nemo se, inquit, decipiat. Si quis se putat sapientem esse in vobis, mundo huic stultus fiat, ut fiat sapiens. Sapientia enim mundi hujus stultitia est apud Deum. Scriptum est enim: Reprehendam sapientes in astutia ipsorum. Et iterum: Cognovit Dominus cogitationes sapientium, quia sunt stultae. Quare, si sapientia illic vera non est, esse non potest et vera patientia. Nam si sapiens ille est qui est humilis et mitis, philosophos autem nec humiles videmus esse nec mites, sed sibi multum placentes, et hoc ipso quod sibi placeant Deo displicentes, apparet illic veram non esse patientiam ubi sit insolens affectatae libertatis audacia et exerti ac seminudi pectoris inverecunda jactantia. Nos autem, fratres dilectissimi, qui philosophi non verbis sed factis sumus, nec vestitu sapientiam, sed veritate praeferimus, qui virtutum conscientiam magis quam jactantiam novimus, qui non loquimur magna sed vivimus, quasi servi et cultores Dei, patientiam quam magisteriis coelestibus discimus obsequiis spiritalibus praebeamus. Est enim nobis cum Deo virtus ista communis. Inde patientia incipit, inde claritas ejus et dignitas caput sumit. Origo et magnitudo patientiae Deo auctore procedit. Diligenda res homini quae Deo chara est: bonum quod amat majestas divina commendat. Si dominus nobis et pater Deus est, sectemur patientiam domini pariter et patris: quia et servos oportet esse obsequentes, et filios non decet esse degeneres. Qualis vero in Deo et quanta patientia, quod, in contumeliam suae majestatis et honoris instituta ab hominibus profana templa et terrena figmenta et sacra sacrilega patientissime sustinens, super bonos et malos aequaliter facit diem nasci et lumen solis oboriri, et cum imbribus terras rigat, nemo a beneficiis ejus excluditur quominus justis similiter et injustis indiscretas pluvias largiatur! Videmus inseparabili aequalitate patientiae nocentibus et innoxiis, religiosis et impiis, gratias agentibus et ingratis, Dei nutu tempora obsequi, elementa famulari, spirare ventos, fontes fluere, grandescere copias messium, fructus maturescere vinearum, exuberare pomis arbusta, nemora frondescere, prata florere. Et cum crebris immo continuis exacerbetur offensis Deus, indignationem suam temperat, et praestitutum semel retributionis diem patienter exspectat. Cumque habeat in potestate vindictam, mavult diu tenere patientiam, sustinens scilicet clementer et differens, ut, si fieri potest, multum malitia protracta aliquando mutetur, et homo in errorum et scelerum contagione volutatus vel sero ad Deum convertatur, ipso monente et dicente: Nolo mortem morientis, quantum ut revertatur et vivat. Et iterum: Revertimini ad me, dicit Dominus. Et iterum: Revertimini ad Dominum Deum vestrum, quoniam misericors et pius et patiens et multae miserationis, et qui sententiam flectat adversus malitias irrogatas. Quod item beatus apostolus Paulus commemorans et peccatorem ad poenitentiam revocans, proponit et dicit: An numquid opulentiam bonitatis ejus et sustinentiam et patientiam contemnis, ignorans quoniam patientia et bonitas Dei ad poenitentiam te adducit? Tu autem, secundum duritiam tuam et cor impoenitens, thesaurizas tibi iram in die irae et revelationis justi judicii Dei, qui reddet unicuique secundum opera sua. Justum judicium Dei dixit esse, quia serum est, quia diu multumque differtur, ut homini ad vitam longa Dei patientia consulatur. Tunc repraesentatur poena impio et peccatori, quando jam non potest poenitentia prodesse peccati.
pass_a_gloss: About to speak on patience, most beloved brothers, and about to preach its advantages and benefits, from where should I rather begin than that now also I see patience to be necessary for your hearing, so that you may not be able to do even this thing that you are hearing and learning without patience. For then at last a salutary sermon and reasoning is effectively learned if what is being said is heard patiently. And I do not find, most beloved brothers, among other heavenly discipline paths by which our sect is directed to attain divine rewards of our hope and faith, what is more useful for life or greater for glory than that we, who lean on the Lord's precepts with obedience of fear and devotion, should especially guard patience with total observation. Even philosophers also profess to follow this. But just as false is patience there, so also is false wisdom. For from where can someone be wise or patient who does not know God's wisdom or patience? When He Himself warns and says about those who seem wise in the world: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent. Also, blessed Apostle Paul, full of the Holy Spirit and sent to call and form the Gentiles, testifies and teaches, saying: See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ, because in Him dwells all the fullness of divinity. And in another place: Let no one deceive himself, he says. If someone among you thinks he is wise, let him become foolish in this world, so that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: I will reprove the wise in their cunning. And again: The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are foolish. Therefore, if wisdom is not true there, true patience cannot exist either. For if the wise one is humble and gentle, but we see that philosophers are neither humble nor gentle, but rather pleasing themselves, and by pleasing themselves, they displease God, it appears that true patience does not exist where there is the audacity of pretended freedom and the shameless boasting of an exerted and half-naked heart. But we, most beloved brothers, who are philosophers not in words but in deeds, and who prefer wisdom not in clothing but in truth, who know the conscience of virtues rather than boasting, who do not speak great things but live them, as servants and worshipers of God, offer patience, which we learn from heavenly teachings, through spiritual obedience. For this virtue is common to us with God. From there, patience begins, from there its clarity and dignity take their start. The origin and greatness of patience proceed from God as author. The thing to be loved by man, which is dear to God, is commended by divine majesty: the good that He loves. If the Lord is our master and Father God, let us follow the patience of the Lord and Father alike, because it is fitting for servants to be obedient, and it is not fitting for sons to be degenerate. But what kind and how great is the patience in God, that, while patiently enduring the profane temples and earthly figments and sacrilegious rites instituted by men in contempt of His majesty and honor, He makes the day rise and the sun's light shine equally over the good and the evil, and with rains, He waters the lands, and no one is excluded from His benefits, so that He lavishes indiscriminate rains on the just and the unjust alike! We see with inseparable equality the patience of God toward the harmful and the innocent, the religious and the impious, those giving thanks and the ungrateful, obeying God's nod, serving the elements, breathing winds, flowing fountains, growing harvests, ripening vineyard fruits, abounding tree fruits, leafing forests, and flowering meadows. And although God is provoked by frequent, indeed continuous, offenses, He tempers His indignation and patiently awaits the predetermined day of retribution. And although He has vengeance in His power, He prefers to hold patience for a long time, sustaining and deferring, so that, if it can be, the malice, having been prolonged, may sometime be changed, and man, having been rolled around in the contagion of errors and crimes, may turn to God, even if late, God Himself warning and saying: I do not want the death of the dying, but that he may turn and live. And again: Turn to me, the Lord says. And again: Turn to the Lord your God, for He is merciful and pious and patient and full of mercy, and He will turn away the sentence against the inflicted malice. Which blessed Apostle Paul also commemorates, recalling the sinner to penitence, and proposes and says: Or do you despise the riches of His goodness and tolerance and patience, ignoring that the patience and goodness of God lead you to penitence? But you, according to your hardness and impenitent heart, treasure up for yourself wrath on the day of wrath and revelation of God's just judgment, who will render to each according to his works. He said that God's just judgment is slow, because it is deferred for a long time, so that God's long patience may consult for man's life. Then punishment is represented to the impious and the sinner, when already penitence can no longer benefit the sin.

pass_b_english: I am about to speak on patience, most beloved brothers, and to proclaim its advantages and benefits. Where should I begin if not with the fact that I see patience as necessary right now for your hearing, so that you cannot even do this thing you are hearing and learning without patience? For a salutary sermon and reasoning is effectively learned only when what is said is heard patiently. I do not find, most beloved brothers, among the other paths of heavenly discipline by which our way is directed toward attaining the divine rewards of our hope and faith, anything more useful for life or greater for glory than that we—who lean on the Lord’s precepts with obedience of fear and devotion—should especially guard patience with total observance. Philosophers also profess to follow this. But their patience is just as false as their wisdom. For how can anyone be wise or patient who does not know the wisdom or patience of God? When He Himself warns about those who seem wise in the world and says: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent” (1 Corinthians 1:19). Also the blessed apostle Paul, full of the Holy Spirit and sent to call and form the Gentiles, testifies and teaches, saying: “See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ, for in Him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:8–9). And in another place: “Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, ‘He catches the wise in their craftiness,’ and again, ‘The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile’” (1 Corinthians 3:18–20). Therefore, if wisdom is not true there, true patience cannot exist either. For if the wise person is humble and gentle, we see that philosophers are neither humble nor gentle, but rather please themselves, and by pleasing themselves they displease God. It is clear that true patience does not exist where there is the audacity of pretended freedom and the shameless boasting of an exerted and half–naked heart. But we, most beloved brothers, are philosophers not in words but in deeds, and we prefer wisdom not in clothing but in truth. We know the conscience of virtues rather than boasting; we do not speak great things but live them, as servants and worshipers of God. Let us offer the patience we learn from heavenly teachings through spiritual obedience. For this virtue is common to us with God. From Him patience begins; from Him its clarity and dignity take their start. The origin and greatness of patience proceed from God as author. A thing to be loved by man, which is dear to God, is commended by divine majesty—the good that He loves. If the Lord is our master and Father, let us follow the patience of the Lord and Father alike, because it is fitting for servants to be obedient, and it is not fitting for sons to be degenerate.

But what kind and how great is the patience in God? He patiently endures the profane temples and earthly fabrications and sacrilegious rites instituted by men in contempt of His majesty and honor. Yet He makes His sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust (Matthew 5:45). No one is excluded from His benefits, so that He lavishes indiscriminate rains on the just and the unjust alike. We see with inseparable equality the patience of God toward the harmful and the innocent, the religious and the impious, those giving thanks and the ungrateful. The elements obey God’s nod and serve: winds breathe, fountains flow, harvests grow, vineyard fruits ripen, trees abound with fruit, forests leaf out, meadows flower. And although God is provoked by frequent, indeed continuous, offenses, He tempers His indignation and patiently awaits the predetermined day of retribution. Though He has vengeance in His power, He prefers to hold patience for a long time, sustaining and deferring, so that, if it can be, the malice, having been prolonged, may sometime be changed, and man, having been rolled around in the contagion of errors and crimes, may turn to God, even if late. God Himself warns and says: “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live” (Ezekiel 18:23; 33:11). And again: “Return to Me,” says the Lord. And again: “Return to the Lord your God, for He is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love, and He relents over disaster” (Joel 2:13). The blessed apostle Paul also commemorates this, recalling the sinner to repentance, and proposes and says: “Or do you presume on the riches of His kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed. He will render to each one according to his works” (Romans 2:4–6). He said that God’s righteous judgment is slow, because it is deferred for a long time, so that God’s long patience may consult for man’s life. Then punishment is represented to the impious and the sinner, when already repentance can no longer benefit the sin.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent English version that correctly incorporates the required inline scripture citations (1 Corinthians 1:19, Colossians 2:8–9, 1 Corinthians 3:18–20, Matthew 5:45, Ezekiel 18:23; 33:11, Joel 2:13, Romans 2:4–6) which were alluded to in the Latin. All clauses, including the descriptions of nature and the theological arguments regarding philosophers, are preserved.
